speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE PRIME
subsubtopic: MINISTER OF AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
In our galleries this afternoon I spy not a stranger but a very good friend, the Right Hon. Gordon Menzies, Prime Minister of Australia.
The applause and enthusiasm greeting Mr. Menzies will convey to him, more than any words of mine, the happiness with which we extend to him a most hearty welcome.
(Translation) ;
We extend to him a most hearty welcome. (Text):
Mr. Menzies has now been prime minister of his vast country for seven and a half years. During his remarkable career, in time of war and peace, he has made many trips around the world, in the course of which we were privileged to have him visit us. In addressing us here in 1941 Mr. Menzies spoke of his eventful journey. At one point he said:
I hope the fact, of which I have been aware, that in three or four places which I visited trouble has since broken out, is no responsibility of mine.
Whenever Mr. Menzies leaves "down under" to come "up over", and vice versa, he spreads on his path nothing but understanding, co-operation, good will and love for peace.
He knows, I am sure, that he will find here between our people and his people complete and unlimited brotherhood. We stood together in time of war; we stand together in time of peace. Having found brotherhood to be so vital to win the war, we want not only to preserve that brotherhood but to use it, strengthened by the leadership of statesmen like Mr. Menzies, in order to ensure peace and safeguard civilization.
He will carry with him the affectionate greetings of the members of this house and the people of Canada to the members of his parliament and to the people of Australia.
50433-119J
May God bless Australia and its distinguished Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to lay on the table copies of a letter I addressed on March 8 to the premiers of the ten provinces with respect to working out arrangements for a federal-provincial fiscal conference this year. In it I proposed to them that we hold a preliminary meeting here in Ottawa shortly after Easter, say April 21 and 22 if those dates are found to be convenient to them, and that this preliminary meeting should be for the purpose of reaching some conclusion on the broad outline of the agenda of the main conference, and to decide upon an opening date.
There are two versions of the letter. The French version was addressed to the premier of Quebec and the English version was sent to the premier of each of the other nine provinces. As was done with the previous correspondence, perhaps hon. members would wish, for the sake of convenience, to have these letters printed as an appendix to the Hansard report of today.

Mr. Speaker, there have been no developments that I know of regarding Formosa and the islands which have altered the position since I answered a question asked on this subject by the hon. member on February 24. Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might endeavour to provide my hon. friend with an oral opinion.
Canada has not included the provinces the hon. member for Greenwood has named, nor, as my colleague the hon. Minister of National Revenue has said, any other provinces for that matter, in these agreements with Ireland or with any other country. In my opinion, to do so would be a quite unwarranted intrusion on the part of Canada into the treasury policies of the provincial governments upon whose behalf Canada, on its own initiative, might presume to make such contract.
It must be remembered that under our constitution the governments and legislatures of the provinces, while acting within their own proper jurisdictions, are just as sovereign as is the government of Canada, and that when a provincial legislature imposes succession duties and income tax it is acting within its jurisdiction.
I suggest the point that my hon. friend from Greenwood, who has just spoken, has overlooked is that every agreement between governments, such as the government of Canada and the government of Ireland, to avoid double taxation of any kind, such as in the case under discussion, to avoid double income tax or double succession duty, is one the express purpose of which is to benefit the taxpayers of the two jurisdictions concerned.
I would point out to my hon. friend that this benefit to the taxpayer is wholly at the expense of the governments which are parties to the agreement to avoid double taxation. And if as the hon. member for Greenwood has suggested Canada were to presume to conclude an agreement, we will say with Ireland, on behalf of Ontario, in order to avoid double taxation, we would be undertaking to reduce the revenues of Ontario without consultation with the government of that province, in a manner which I suggest the hon. member for Greenwood himself, upon reflection, would regard as wholly indefensible.
Now, quite apart from the fact that we have no constitutional authority for presuming to reduce the revenues of a provincial government in this way, we think such an act on our part would be an unwarranted interference with the treasury policy of the province

Income Tax
concerned. To demonstrate in a practical way why this is so, perhaps it might be more clear to my hon. friend from Greenwood if I were to take a hypothetical case and, in order to simplify that case, leave Canada out of the picture altogether and consider a hypothetical agreement between the province of Ontario and Ireland.
In order to put this in practical form, let us suppose there is a Mr. Ireland domiciled in Ireland who has property in Ontario on which the succession duty to Ontario, because the property is located there, would be $200, and on which Ontario property Mr. Ireland, living in Ireland, would also have to pay $200 by way of succession duty to Ireland, because of being domiciled there. At the same time let us suppose there is a Mr. Ontario domiciled in Ontario who has property in Ireland upon which the Irish succession duty is $200 and upon which because he is domiciled in Ontario the Ontario succession duty is $200.
I am suggesting that, in the absence of an agreement, on these facts Ireland would collect $400, of which $200 would arise from the fact that Mr. Ireland is domiciled in Ireland and $200 from the fact that Mr. Ontario has property in Ireland. Ontario likewise would collect $400, of which $200 will be from Mr. Ontario because he is domiciled in Ontario and the other $200 will be upon property Mr. Ireland has in Ontario. In other words there will be double taxation as a result of which the government of Ontario and the government of Ireland will each get the sum of $400.
If an arrangement to avoid double taxation were entered into between the two governments concerned the result would be that each government would get only the tax upon the property located within its boundaries. That is, they would each get $200, and the taxpayers in Ireland and in Ontario would likewise pay only $200. The $200 which would be saved to each of the taxpayers would be at the expense of the two governments concerned.
My hon. friend has been criticizing the government of Canada because in dealing with Ireland it has not undertaken on behalf of Ontario to reduce the revenues of Ontario by concluding a treaty for that purpose with Ireland, and notwithstanding that the government of Ontario has not requested such a treaty. I believe that if the hon. member, as the former general manager of a trust company, would reflect upon the situation he would agree that it would be an unwarranted act upon our part to presume to do what he has suggested in relation to the
[Mr. Garson.l
sovereign powers of the province of Ontario over its own treasury policy. If Ontario wants to enter into a contract to avoid double taxation, as a result of which, while the taxpayers may benefit, the government of Ontario itself will lose substantial sums of money from its treasury, surely that is a matter which should be left to the sovereign authority of the province of Ontario.

He asks why we should not approach the Ontario government and suggest to it that at the time that we conclude a treaty to avoid double taxation with another country, we should include Ontario in that treaty. My answer to that question is that for two reasons we should not do so. The first of those reasons is that, having regard to the fact that the government and legislature of a province now exercising their provincial powers under our constitution are just as sovereign as are the government and parliament of Canada, it would in my opinion be quite improper for us to make

to that government a suggestion volunteered by us that it had not sought that it change its provincial treasury policy in relation to a matter which is wholly within its own provincial jurisdiction. The relevant provision which was read into the record by my colleague reads as follows:
Where estate, legacy or succession duty is paid by an Ontario resident to any jurisdiction which has been designated by the lieutenant governor in council, the duty levied in Ontario shall be reduced by the amount of duty so paid in the foreign jurisdiction which does not exceed the amount of duty levied in Ontario. This allowance is granted whether the other jurisdiction grants similar relief to its residents in respect of Ontario duties or not, though formerly it was granted only if the foreign jurisdiction reciprocated. The jurisdictions designated by regulation 33 include Great Britain and Northern Ireland, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Eire, Quebec, the District of Columbia, and the states of the United States of America. Regulation 33 was first established by order in council on June 21, 1946. It is now incorporated into the consolidated regulations.
Therefore, far from our having to intrude into the affairs of Ontario in order, as my hon. friend suggested in his remarks the other day, to protect citizens of Canada resident in Ontario, the fact was that at the time he was making his speech they were already protected by Ontario regulations.

If I intervene in this debate it is to point out that if this amendment were carried it would undoubtedly make our relations with Ireland much more difficult. Earlier in this discussion some reference was made to delicacy of constitutional approach. I can think of nothing less delicate, from the point of view of our relations with the government of Ireland, than the adoption of an amendment of this kind which would make extremely difficult, if not impossible, the negotiation and signing of agreements with that country.
To support that position, Mr. Speaker, I must put on the record what I think is the factual situation with regard to the designation of this state with which we are negotiating this agreement. As my hon. friend who has just spoken has pointed out, it is true that between 1921 and 1927 the 26 counties of southern Ireland were known as the Irish Free State. It is also true that the Irish constitution, adopted in 1937, stated- I think it is article 4-that the name of the state is Eire or, in the English language, Ireland. That is how these people have designated their own state in their own constitution. I submit that is the proper designation because it is the constitutional one.
Article 2 of this constitution states that the national territory consists of the whole island of Ireland: but article 3 in the constitution provides that pending-and I think these are the words of the article-reintegration of the national territory as so described, the laws enacted by the Irish parliament are to be limited in application to the area of the 26 counties.
Then in 1949 Ireland severed her last remaining link with the crown by a statute which is named, it is true, the Republic of Ireland Act. It is also true that that act declared that the description of the state shall be the Republic of Ireland. However, I believe that this does not change the name of the state as established by the constitution, which could only be changed by a constitutional amendment.

In the years that have passed the succeeding Liberal administrations have tampered considerably with this worthy concept. They now have, among other things, an organization which monopolizes the field of network radio in Canada, far and away the most lucrative of all fields of radio, an organization which largely monopolizes television in Canada and completely monopolizes the major centres of Canada in which television is now being presented. Other members of the house, notably the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, have explored some aspects of the problem quite thoroughly previously in this debate. In the opportunity now offered me I should like to go a little further afield and present certain information which may be of value to the committee in its examination of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the various facets of its operations.
The first point I should like to make concerns the somewhat slap-happy use of funds by the corporation and, shall we say, the somewhat questionable ways in which some of these funds are being spent. I turn now to one specific instance which I shall develop in some detail because in my opinion it shows quite clearly what the government has developed in this field and what the corporation is doing with the funds placed at its disposal by the government. The argument I wish to develop has to do with the association of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with an organization commonly known as CAPAC, its full name being the Composers, Authors and Publishers Association of Canada Limited.
This organization has for its purpose the licensing of musical performance rights for use by radio stations and other organizations. The revenue from these sources is then remitted to the publishers, authors and composers with, as far as can be ascertained, the greater portion of the revenues going directly to the publishers. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been uniformly and surprisingly generous in its dealings with this
Special Committee on Broadcasting body. The interesting thing about it is that at the present time, having two broad fields of radio broadcasting in Canada, one the C.B.C. and the other the private stations, we find that the C.B.C. makes payments to CAPAC on a substantially different and more generous basis than do the private radio stations of Canada, despite the fact that the purpose of these payments is exactly the same in each case.
For proof of this I turn to the Canada Gazette of January 29, 1954, in which is published the schedule of payments to CAPAC. We find there tariff No. 2 covering radio broadcasting, section (a) of which is as follows:
By the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for all broadcasts from stations owned or controlled by it a fee of one cent per capita of the population of Canada as latest reported by the dominion bureau of statistics, plus a sum equal to 12 per cent of the gross revenue as hereinafter defined . . .
Then there are a few words indicating the financial statement which is to be used. Section (b) reads as follows:
By each other licensee of the association for all broadcasts from the station owned or operated by such licensee a sum equal to 13 per cent of the gross revenue as hereinafter defined . . .
Reference is then made to the financial cutoff date. We have here a clear case of the C.B.C. paying one cent per capita to this organization, which amount is not paid by the private radio stations. I may say, and I shall develop it further shortly, that the tariff would have been substantially higher if it had not been that the private radio stations had to make a case in their own defence which ultimately benefited the C.B.C. as well as themselves.
Looking at the history of this particular agreement we find that when the existing tariff was established CAPAC requested from the privately-owned broadcasting stations eight-tenths of a cent per capita plus 2\ per cent of the gross revenue, and from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation one cent plus 2j per cent of their gross revenue. This proposition was strongly opposed by the private radio stations but the C.B.C. position- remember, this is an expenditure of public funds made by the C.B.C.-is set out by Mr. Peter Wright, counsel for the corporation, in the proceedings before the copyright appeal board on January 23 and 24, 1952. It will be found at page 660, and is as follows:
The attitude of the C.B.C. has been made perfectly clear in all the hearings and in the briefs, namely, that CAPAC had advanced a tariff, and we have looked at it, and we are advancing no objection.
Again Mr. Wright says at page 665:
That is why I have been particularly solicitous not to take a position before the board, and not

Special Committee on Broadcasting to examine Mr. Allard, because my position was that the tariff was in the Gazette, that we had read it, and that we had no objection to it.
With that sort of attitude it is easy to see that if it had not been for the work and effort of the private radio stations the original demands of CAP AC would have been met and agreed to. Actually the position was that after some two weeks of debate carried almost completely by the private radio stations the agreement I set forth originally was arrived at, namely that the C.B.C. and the private radio stations would each pay If per cent of their gross revenue and the C.B.C. would pay an additional one cent per capita of population.
This final agreement, Mr. Speaker, in comparison with the originally proposed agreement, represents an annual saving of hundreds of thousands of dollars to the radio stations, both private and C.B.C. In the case of the C.B.C. this is a direct saving of many tens of thousands of dollars which benefits the taxpayers, yet this is money which the corporation would willingly, as the statements quoted show, have thrown away.
Having established the fact that the C.B.C. is prepared to deal more generously with CAPAC with public funds than the private broadcasters seemed to deem wise, let us have a look at how this money is used. This is important in examining the attitude of the C.B.C. If CAPAC were essentially a Canadian organization dispensing its funds in Canada it is possible that the attitude of the C.B.C. would be justified, on the grounds of encouraging Canadian talent and offering such talent adequate remuneration. This is simply not the case. CAPAC is primarily an extension into Canada of a United States organization known as ASCAP. The full name shows a remarkable similarity, in that it is the American society of authors, composers and publishers.
I shall not go into all the details, for the relationship between these two organizations was set forth quite adequately, I believe, back in 1947. When the United States of America proceeded in court against ASCAP they named the Canadian CAPAC as one of the co-conspirators in the particular action they were taking. We must realize also that CAPAC could only be an extension of the United States organization because of the fact that the United States organization controls the great bulk of the music performed on radio stations in that country and the great bulk of music performed over Canadian radio stations as well.
Turning then to what happened, having shown the relationship between the Canadian


organization and the United States organization and established the fact that this relationship exists, let us see what happens to these funds which are paid by the C.B.C. to the CAPAC organization in Canada. In that connection I should like to give certain quotations from the Broadcasting-Telecasting magazine of April 13, 1953. We find there that Mr. Louis Bernstein, treasurer of the United States organization, reported to the society's annual meeting that their total revenue included $1,329,400 collected for performances of ASCAP music abroad. Later on in the same article the following statement is made:
Last fall, Mr. Bernstein said, ASCAP members got $390,000 in royalties for broadcasting rights to ASCAP music in England and Canada.
Since the revenue to this Canadian source, CAPAC, was approximately $718,000 in 1953, of which the great majority came from radio stations; since we have seen the relationship between this organization and the United States organization; that funds are paid by the Canadian organization to the United States organization, and that the commodity which the Canadian organization is selling is so largely a United States commodity, I think we are quite justified in assuming that the payments being made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to this organization are being very largely funnelled off into the United States. The point in that connection is that various estimates have been made-CAPAC does not publish detailed financial statements of the money it pays out- by informed people, ranging as high as 90 per cent of the revenue of this body being diverted to the United States.
I want to turn now to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the government. I ask them to enter at some point before this committee a defence of such an iniquitous agreement by which, first, the corporation pays on a totally different basis from private radio stations; second, not only does it pay on a totally different basis from private radio stations but it pays it through an organization which essentially is doing very little for the development of Canadian culture, Canadian artists, Canadian composers or Canadian anything else. I feel that the great bulk of the people with whom I have talked who know something about the operation of radio in Canada believe that the C.B.C. has a legitimate function in the development of Canadian talent, as do the private radio stations, who have done an outstanding job in the field. Most informed people view that function as one in which payments

are made directly to Canadian authors, directly to Canadian composers, directly to Canadian artists, and the money kept in Canada. This is not the case under the agreement.
I should like to say just one or two words more about CAPAC before I leave it. The board of directors is not entirely Canadian. Four out of the existing 12 directors give as their addresses various points in the United States. There is some indication that other directors are representative of other groups in other parts of the world. I was interested in finding on that directorial body in 1951 a civil servant of long standing. I think we may just leave it there, Mr. Speaker. It is a peculiar arrangement, because it certainly is not to the benefit of either Canadian talent or the Canadian taxpayer.
I turn now for a moment to the delay in establishing television stations in the major Canadian centres. In that connection I should like to first remind the house of the indefinite attitude of the government at various times when the question has come up. When will a station operated by a private organization be established in Montreal or Toronto? The government has never been very definite about that, but it has been most hopeful. It has held out the promise that in the indefinite but very near future we will have such a station.
Let us view that promise in the light of certain information which has recently become available. I quote from the March 4 issue of Marketing, at page 20, where I find the report of a television forum held in Montreal, one of the participants being Mr. W. E. Powell, commercial manager of the C.B.C. There is this section I would like to quote:
Powell was also asked, "When, if ever, is the C.B.C. going to amend its policy of one TV station to one major market?"
"It is not C.B.C. policy: it is government policy. I do not know."
"Isn't it government policy based on C.B.C. recommendations?"
"It is government policy to extend the television network across Canada first."
Having said that I turn to Hansard, and I find the minister's statement at page 1806 where, halfway down the first column, we find this:
It is expected that the complete coast to coast service will be in operation in about three years, with portions to be completed well before that.
I am not going to delve into this aspect any more, but I do wish to put these quotations on record so people in these cities will know that, according to those quotations, the government has not the slightest intention of installing for at least three years private T.V. in Montreal, Toronto or any of the other major centres asking for it. I think that should
Special Committee on Broadcasting be a matter of record, and I would like the government to stand up to it and, if that is their intention, to say so.
Then, going back to that quotation for a moment but in relation to another subject- it is most interesting, because one gets all sorts of things out of it-let us compare the minister's statement in the house on March 7 when he said:
Because of the nature of broadcasting the C.B.C. has been placed by statute In a position in which it is not responsible to a minister of the crown in carrying out its activities. It is answerable to parliament itself. Quite differently from my own department, for instance, I am not responsible for the general activities of the C.B.C.
Yet let us compare the last three sentences of the quotation to which I referred-and I shall repeat them so they may be compared with what the minister said-with the minister's assumption that the C.B.C. is a little entity unto itself, of which he knows very little and over which he has very little control. Here we have one of the representatives of the C.B.C., Mr. Powell, saying:
It is not C.B.C. policy: it is government policy. I do not know.
And then this question:
Isn't it government policy based on C.B.C. recommendations?
The foregoing statement is substantially what is found in the minister's statement. Mr. Powell's answer is:
It is government policy to extend the television network across Canada first.
In other words, no matter what face may be put upon it by the government either in the house or elsewhere, the operators of the C.B.C. are very much aware of who cracks the whip. And it is the government that cracks the whip. It is the operating personnel of the C.B.C. who, I imagine, very often subordinate their own interests and their own decisions to follow the direction of the government-and in considerable more detail than the government admits.
If we examine this further, there is a most interesting comparison that can be made between the statement of the minister responsible for this corporation in the house, as he placed it before hon. members on March 7, and what was said in an address by Mr. Dunton, chairman of the board of governors, on December 26. Now, here is the minister who got up in the house, in his original statement, and in his sweet innocence disclaimed responsibility for the operation of the C.B.C. He said they were responsible to parliament, and that he really did not have anything to do with it. In fact he could not answer at all many of the questions about the C.B.C., and that of course has been obvious for many years. I can only say in that respect, Mr. Speaker, that it may well be a carefully thought out policy of the government that they should have placed the C.B.C. under the direction of the Minister of National Revenue, who collects the great bulk of the taxation from the people of Canada. That is the minister's statement. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is the type of state visualized oy George Orwell in his book entitled "1984". That is the type of thinking they had. Why should the government decide what television will bring into the Canadian home? Does the government not trust the Canadian people? Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate we have heard hon. members refer to the talks over the C.B.C. as being sometimes to


the left, sometimes to the right and sometimes to the centre. Judging by the length of some of the speeches we have heard by members of the Progressive Conservative party I would suggest, if I may use the terminology of an old steam engineer, that a lot of them have got on centre and have not been able to get off.
My remarks will be brief. Primarily I rose to associate myself with members of this group and other hon. members in the house in supporting the motion that the government set up a select committee to look into the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As a member of that committee I look forward with some anticipation to its deliberations.
My knowledge of radio broadcasting relates more to the technical aspects than to anything else, but I hasten to add that that knowledge is extremely limited. However, that limited knowledge permits me to question the proposition put forward by hon. members in relation to broadcasting, as to who shall or who shall not be responsible for broadcasting in this country. They advance that question in an effort to establish what agency would likely bring about the most desirable end result. According to a lot of hon. members the end result is culture, whatever that means. I always panic whenever I hear the word.
There are 150 private broadcasting stations operating in Canada. The critics of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation lament the fact that they are in competition with the C.B.C., but I think that is a debatable point. If they are in competition with the C.B.C. I maintain that they are in that position because the C.B.C. has made it possible for them to be in that position. I am always amazed when I hear organizations lamenting that they are being discriminated against because they cannot get into some lucrative field which someone else has spent a great deal of time, money and energy in developing. I maintain that the private stations operating in Canada at the moment are enjoying a pretty lucrative business from a dollar and cents point of view.
I repeat that had it not been for the C.B.C., in my opinion the only agency that could possibly have established in the first instance the kind of broadcasting system we have in this country, we would not be enjoying the quality and type of program that is presently being presented. A recent survey carried out in the United States-and I have no reason to believe that Canada is different-indicates that regional revenues are falling off but that local advertising is increasing by leaps and bounds.

Something was said to the effect that local broadcasting stations are able to further the interests of local talent, and so forth. I submit that that is not done to an extent commensurate with the increased revenues they are enjoying. The Massey commission reported that the private owners of broadcasting as an industry and their stations hardly rate a pass on cultural programs. They stated that too many stations regulated in principle by the C.B.C. offer programs which must be described as regrettable. In a sampling of five stations there was no attempt to fulfil the proper function of the local station, to reflect the life and interests of the community and to use and develop local talent available. They reported that spot announcements crowd their programs. Only very rarely can limited revenue be advanced as an extenuating circumstance for this inexpensive and unimaginative programming.
There is criticism that the talks are always a form of propaganda. I suppose that is true, and I suppose also many people would put forward the proposition that the sermon on the mount is propaganda. In my opinion that is a very weak argument to put forth. Whether the talks are biased to the right or to the left I do not think should be of any concern.
I have not mentioned television because I feel that at the present time at any rate there are many factors which make it imperative that the control of television remain vested in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. One factor to be considered is the limited number of channels available. I think most important of all is the fact that television can create tremendous impressions for good or evil. I am not going to say anything about operating revenue, because I think possibly some revisions will be brought about during the course of the committee hearings. I am sure these questions will be fully investigated.

As I say, there are two things I should like to comment on, one of which I have commented on before. In this connection I should like to quote from page 282 of the Massey report as follows:
Special Committee on Broadcasting The principal complaint is that the C.B.C., ". . . is at one and the same time competitor, regulator, prosecutor, jury and judge".
It is very hard for me to understand how reasonable men can go on maintaining that situation. I think we can understand how it arose originally, and indeed I fully expect that I shall have it cast up at me that a great leader of the party to which I belong at one time was in favour of it. But that is a good many years ago. Radio has developed beyond the dreams of those days. It is the situation of today with which we are dealing. If I remember aright, when I raised this point on previous occasions the minister answered me by reference to the Massey report. I want to read a paragraph of the Massey report because it seems to me that, in purporting to deal with the complaint that I make, they do not deal with it at all. All they say is-and with this I fully agree- that there should be regulation. What I am complaining about is the kind of regulation.
Here let me interject what I intended to say at the outset; I want to make this very clear. I am a great believer in the C.B.C. I admire a great deal of the work they do. I think we ought to be grateful for the work they do. My leader has gone out of his way to praise the work they do. What I am complaining about is government action in creating two situations which I think are wholly unsound.
The first is the dual character of competitor and regulator. I want to read from page 283 of the Massey report because I think the argument which they make and which they seem to think justifies the present control does nothing whatever, I suggest, to justify the present control but merely justifies control, of which we are all in favour. I read from page 283:
Broadcasting in Canada, in our view, is a public service directed and controlled in the public interest by a body responsible to parliament.
I am all in favour of that.
Private citizens are permitted to engage their capital and their energies in this service, subject to the regulations of this body. That these citizens should be assured of just and eaual treatment, that they should enjoy adeauate security or compensation for the actual monetary investments they are permitted to make, is apparent. We shall have recommendations to make on this matter later. But that they enjoy any vested right to engage in broadcasting as an industry, or that they have any status except as part of the national broadcasting system, is to us inadmissible.
It seems to me they get involved in a hopeless confusion there. They seem to me to confuse the national broadcasting system- that is to say the regulatory body as it

This system is not one whit more reasonable than the one you would have if you created a situation whereby the Canadian National Railways had full power over the Canadian Pacific Railway. The situation is absolutely on all fours. I can see no difference whatever. All I can say is that when a good man goes wrong, sometimes he goes terribly wrong. I want to quote from what he said when the bill was passed in 1952-53, as reported at page 4185 of Hansard of April 21, 1953;
It is therefore proposed that the Canadian Broadcasting Act should be amended to provide that the corporation should in future receive from month to month the amount of revenue yielded by the present 15 per cent special excise tax on television sets and the picture tubes for such sets, . . .

And later:
In this way those who buy sets, or the replacement tubes for them, will be providing the basic revenue necessary for C.B.C. television services.

I should add that the idea behind this proposal-if there really was an idea of any kind behind it-was that those who used the service should pay for it. It was thought apparently that in this way some kind of rough justice was going to be achieved. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that you might as well-take any ridiculous illustration you like-for example say that the people inhabiting jails should pay for the upkeep of the jails because they are the people who are receiving the benefit. I deliberately take a ridiculous situation because this thing is so ridiculous.
By some happy accident that nobody could have foreseen, it might have worked out that the amount which the C.B.C. received in this fantastic manner would have been just about the amount which they needed. If that had happened, the absurdity of this arrangement might not have become so apparent. I think it is a good thing that it did not turn out that way. I am still hoping that as time goes on the absurdity of this thing will become apparent and that when it becomes sufficiently apparent and the ministers are in a good mood, it will be changed.
Actually what has happened is, as we all know, that television sets have sold much more freely than was anticipated, and the results have been to give the corporation much more money than was intended. Of course what has happened is what happens to us all when we get more money than we should have: We come to be careless with the money. The hon. member for Eglinton pointed out something which interested me greatly yesterday, namely the two-year delay in referring the matter to a chartered accountant for advice. I am not surprised that there was two years' delay. I would have thought that they might be hesitating even yet to bring this absurd situation to the attention of serious men.
I want to point out one or two of the obvious absurdities which have arisen by reason of the easy money which they have been receiving. First of all, I should point out that their income in the year 1953-54, as has been pointed out, was $27,431,000, of

which 84 per cent was derived from taxation.
If my arithmetic is correct, that means that about $23 million came from taxation and the rest was earned.
We now have this beautiful irony. In the statement we find that they have an operating surplus. I think that is what they call it. They have an operating surplus of $6,500,000. In a financial set-up so extraordinary and so unusual it may be that they experienced difficulty in finding words to describe the situation; but for an organization with an income of $27 million, 84 per cent of which is derived from taxation, to announce that it has an operating surplus of $6,500,000 is something that I should think would make an ordinary accountant jump out of his skin.
I think an accountant who has to deal with this situation is going to have a job on his hands.
To give another fantastic illustration, because the whole thing is fantastic, I suppose we may roughly describe the Canadian people as the shareholders of this corporation. I will make a very brief statement. As the terms of the resolution indicate, there are two matters provided for in this resolution which precedes the introduction of a bill. The first is to extend the life of the Defence Production Act. Hon. members know, and the resolution indicates, that under a section of the act as it now exists the major portion of the act-that is, except subsection 6 of section 4-would expire on July 31, 1956. It will be proposed in the bill to follow the adoption of this resolution, if and when it is adopted, to delete that clause and not have any limitation upon the duration of the statute itself. At the same time, the bill to follow this resolution will propose an adjustment in the salary of the Minister of Defence Production for the purpose of bringing it into conformity with the Salaries Act as amended at the last session of parliament. Of course that has no immediate effect because hon. members know that the Minister of Defence Production is at the same time the Minister of Trade and Commerce and draws only the salary provided for that department, though he has the responsibility of the two.
It is felt that there should be conformity between the provisions of that statute and the Salaries Act, and the bill will provide for the appropriate amendment. But the main amendment is the repeal of section 41, which provides for the expiry of the act, and therefore for the winding up of the Department of Defence Production on July 31, 1956. This amendment is being introduced to extend the life of the department so that it may operate on a more permanent basis. We feel that there are a number of reasons for recommending this action at this time.
Hon. members will recall that when the Department of Defence Production was established on April 1, 1951, it was to meet an


emergency situation brought to a head by the fighting in Korea. At that time it was impossible to predict how long the need for greatly increased military defence procurements would continue. To meet the immediate situation, the government embarked on a 3-year defence preparedness program which it was later found necessary to extend because of the circumstances which continued to exist. Procurement machinery to carry out this was established on a short-term basis. Almost 4 years have elapsed since the Department of Defence Production was set up and it is now apparent that the temporary character of the department is neither in keeping with the international outlook nor satisfactory from an administrative point of view.
As far as the need for a separate department responsible for the production and supply of Canada's military requirements is concerned, the situation has not changed. The peak of the defence program is past-at least we hope that what is past will prove to be the real peak, that will at no time be exceeded-but it is levelling off at a relatively high level and the magnitude of the program is such that we feel it should not be left to the responsibility of crown agencies or branches of other departments with important functions of their own to perform.
Furthermore, the complexity of modern weapons and defence supplies is such that a sizeable organization is required to handle defence procurement and production. The technological developments in the last few decades have of course stirred the imagination of all of us, but they proved to be very costly, and this is particularly true in the field of aircraft and electronics. To translate these developments from the drawing board to the production line is a major problem and one which affects those responsible for procurement as well as those charged with the manufacture of defence requirements. Additional complications arise from the fact that modern aircraft and ships contain highly complex armament and electronic equipment. Close co-ordination is essential in the different procurement fields of aircraft, shipbuilding, electronics, ammunition and guns as well as in some of the more normal commercial fields.
To carry out production and procurement to meet Canada's present sizeable and complex defence program requires a department staffed by competent and experienced officials. Hon. members will appreciate that it is difficult to attract and retain high-calibre civil service personnel in a department that is looked upon as temporary, that is to say, to have them come there for an indefinite

time, and that is particularly true in peacetime. When the situation is really critical, well, the critical nature of the situation weighs heavily in the minds of those who make their services available for the benefit of their fellow citizens. But when it extends as something which nevertheless becomes a semi-permanent feature of the necessary requirements, it is desirable, we feel, to have some permanent character to the organization.
So far, the Department of Defence Production has been quite fortunate in this respect, but it is felt that the time has come when the life of the department should be extended by placing it on the same basis as other government departments, leaving it to parliament to decide if and when it will be proper to bring it to a termination.
I am sure there is no need to point out the satisfactory manner in which the Department of Defence Production has carried out its defence procurement functions. The record is such that I am sure hon. members will agree that, in line with the principle of procurement by a non-military agency of the requirements of the armed services and in the interests of good administration and efficient operation, the Department of Defence Production should continue at this time to carry out these functions. The proposed amendment covers only those two points that I have mentioned.
To those who are not keenly aware of the problems which must be faced continuously in the field of defence procurement the question might arise as to why an act set up in an emergency should continue to contain broad powers of responsibility when the life of the act is being extended indefinitely. I would point out that many of these powers are required to complete the present program- the aircraft portion of that program now extends at least into 1960-and to carry out the continuing functions of the department.
There are other powers which are not being used at this time but which were placed there because they were considered to be essential in dealing with any emergency which might arise and which might interfere with the regular production and procurement of what was necessary to build up our forces and to discharge our commitments to our associates in this joint undertaking.
In the present unsettled state of international affairs I do not feel that the time has come to take out of the act those powers which are there and which enable the department to deal expeditiously with any situation that would interfere with the regular maintenance of Canada's defensive strength and the regular carrying out of Canada's undertaking.

The bill which will follow the adoption of this resolution will provide those two things, the adjustment of the salary to the scale fixed by the Salaries Act adopted at the last session and the elimination of this section which would otherwise bring the act to a termination and require the winding up of the department on July 31, 1956.

Mr. Chairman, it is a fact which I am sure is appreciated by all hon. members that when a resolution is required to precede a bill it usually asks approval for the introduction of a bill only so far as it is required, and in that event there may normally be in the bill other provisions than those indicated in the resolution. I am sure that many of us had hoped that the Prime Minister would indicate in his statement that the bill to be introduced would contain more than the two provisions mentioned in the resolution and would have the effect of bringing before the house some modification of the sweeping provisions of the Defence Production Act.
However, the Prime Minister has made it abundantly clear that the bill to follow the present resolution will purport to do two things and two things only, namely, increase the salary of the minister from $10,000 to $15,000 per annum and repeal section 41 of the act.
I shall not attempt at this moment to put myself in the position which one might be in when we come to deal with the second reading of the bill and are confronted with the principle of the bill. However, I have some observations to make which I think are necessarily called for in the light of the statement the Prime Minister has made today.
So far as the salary of the minister is concerned, I take it that this is not a very far-reaching matter. As the Prime Minister has indicated, the effect of this amendment will be to bring the salary of the Minister of Defence Production into line with the salaries provided by all other relevant statutes for all other cabinet ministers. Of course it raises the question whether there is in the mind of the Prime Minister some thought of detaching this particular portfolio from that of trade and commerce, in view of the fact that since its inception it has been held by the same minister.

Defence Production Act The effect of the proposal to repeal section 41 of the Defence Production Act is virtually to ask the house to re-enact one of the most important statutes on the statute books of this parliament, a statute which extends to some 22 pages and embraces 40 operative sections. It is perhaps a curious fact that so much will be accomplished by such a brief provision. The bill by simply providing that section 41 of the act is repealed will be equivalent to the re-enactment for an indefinite period by this parliament of the extensive provisions of a most important statute.
I do not at this point intend to undertake any review of the administration of the department. There is much in the administration that will not commend the present measure. The Prime Minister has spoken of the part which this department has played in the defence program. It has played an important part indeed because through this department billions of dollars have been expended in the defence effort. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition have had reason to think and have put evidence before the house to show that much of that expenditure has been made very loosely. There was much evidence of that before the defence expenditure committee two years ago. However, there may be another opportunity to go into the question of administration.
The Prime Minister has asked the house to give permanence to the department and to the provisions of the act. That should take our thoughts back to the circumstances under which this measure was passed. It was four years ago, in the month of March, 1951, that the house was dealing with a resolution and with a bill which eventually took shape in the act. That was just nine months after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea. Along with 15 other nation members of the United Nations Canada with her armed forces was participating in resisting communist aggression in Korea. The hostilities had passed through some climacteric stages even at that time. Successes and reverses had alternated for the arms of the United Nations and a crisis of major proportions confronted the western world.
The Prime Minister has pointed out today that we have not passed from the atmosphere of crisis in the world. I am not going to dispute the assertion that there is still an atmosphere and indeed some reality of crisis in the world today. Its form has changed not a little since March, 1951, but there are other circumstances which weighed heavily upon the House of Commons four years ago in relation to this measure.
What we were confronted with at that time was a world scramble for strategic

Defence Production Act supplies or for the construction or operation of defence projects ,or by way of advance payment on account of or to enable that person to carry out any contract entered into with the minister under this act or any defence contract; and
-(g) do all such things as appear to the minister to be incidental to or necessary or expedient to the matters mentioned in the foregoing provisions of this section or as may be authorized by the governor in council with respect to the procurement, construction or disposal of defence supplies or defence projects.
It is hard* sir, in contemplating these provisions to conceive of anything that could be wider in scope and in the power they confer upon the minister. Under section 16 power is given to establish a defence production revolving fund under which provision is made for $100 million being placed at the disposal of the minister as a revolving fund, and we know that revolving fund has been used over and over again. Under section 17 the minister is given power to enter into contracts in many cases without tender. Section 17, subsection 1 (e), provides that the minister may enter into a contract without the approval of the governor in council if in his opinion the contract must be entered into immediately in the interests of defence or the estimated expenditure does not exceed $25,000 or, if tenders have been obtained, involving an estimated expenditure not exceeding $50,000.
Then we have the provisions of section 23 and the following sections. Under section 23 the minister has power, where any person whom he requests to enter into a defence contract on terms that the minister considers fair and reasonable has refused or failed to enter into such contract, to direct that person to produce, deliver or store, or to construct, as the case may be, on terms and conditions that appear to the minister to be fair and reasonable, the defence supplies or the defence project or projects that would have been the subject matter of the contract. In other words, where anyone called upon by the minister to accept a defence contract does not wish to do so, the minister has absolute powers to compel him to do so.
Under section 24 the minister is given power to requisition for defence purposes defence supplies of any kind. Under section 26 the minister has the power to determine priority of production on the part of anyone engaged in defence production. Under section 27 the minister is given power to appoint a controller with sweeping powers to occupy any of these defence undertakings and to operate them as an agent of the minister. That power exists in any case where a person has failed to satisfy the minister that in the performance of a defence contract he has been carrying it out in a businesslike and efficient manner, or where
tMr. Fleming.]
a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed to keep proper and detailed records of the cost, or where a person to whom a direction has been given under section 23, which I mentioned earlier, has failed to comply with it in the view of the minister.
Under section 28 the minister has power to relieve any person from other legal obligations if he is called upon to enter into a defence contract with the minister. Under section 29 the minister is given wide powers to direct an investigation into the affairs of anyone entering into a contract to supply defence materials or construct defence projects. Under section 30 the governor in council may from time to time designate as essential materials or essential services whatever materials and substances or whatever activities are in his opinion essential. Under section 31 the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he deems necessary to control and regulate the production, processing, distribution, acquisition, disposition or use of essential materials or the supply or use of essential services for the purpose of ensuring the availability of defence supplies or the construction or operation of defence projects, or to ensure that abnormal requirements of essential materials for defence supplies or defence projects are obtained in the manner least likely to cause disruption of the trade and commerce of the country.
There are teeth in this act. Section 32 attaches to breaches of the act, or of the orders made by the minister under the provisions of the act, penalties which extend tc two years' imprisonment and fines up tc $5,000. Under section 39 the governor in council is given power to make orders and regulations to carry out the purposes and provisions of the act.
There, sir, in a brief and quite inadequate way, is a sketchy review of powers as absolute and as sweeping in their nature as are to be found anywhere in any Canadian legislation, the only counterpart in this country being the provisions of the War Measures Act, which is brought into effect only in time of war, and the Emergency Powers Act, the sister measure which accompanied this legislation in the early days of the Korean crisis and which was permitted to expire last year with no harm felt by anyone.
It may be that the minister will ask the house to justify continuation of powers as sweeping as these on the ground that it is necessary to have stand-by powers. Stand-by for what purpose? A crisis? Well, the kind

of crisis that could justify the continuation on a mere stand-by basis of powers like these is surely that kind of crisis, and that kind of crisis only, which is contemplated in the provisions of the War Measures Act. We do not wish to see powers retained by the minister which could be used by him as a club over the heads of Canadians. There is very great danger of that threatening club existing as long as powers as broad as these are retained by any minister in time of peace or even of cold war. Indeed, these powers are so broad that no businessman or manufacturer is in a position to stand up to the minister if the minister has made up his mind on anything affecting that manufacturer, if it relates in any way to the construction of any materials or projects that have any relationship whatever to what the minister may regard as the defence program.
These are not the times for permitting the continuance, Mr. Speaker, of powers so sweeping that those whose plants or whose materials are related in any way to defence must stand in fear of an omnipotent government. Let me make it quite clear that these powers are a carryover from the days of crisis, days when we appeared to stand and were told by the government that we stood on the very brink of being plunged into war. These are powers that are a carryover from a time when defence materials were in critically short supply, and not only our country but other countries in the world were engaged in a feverish scramble to obtain strategic materials at virtually any price and upon any conditions. These powers are a carryover also from a time, as I suggested earlier, when we had not advanced in any measure at all on the rearmament program. It was barely beginning then.
It was Korea, which had exposed to the western world in ugly naked form the grave dangers that did confront the western world, which led this parliament by unanimous decision to embark upon a costly rearmament program, which all of us regretted but which all of us felt to be necessary in the kind of world in which we found ourselves. We have advanced a long way on the defence program since those days. The program upon which billions of dollars have been spent has proceeded a long way. Surely no hon. member is going to assert in this house that the conditions that are faced today by the government in the continuation of the defence program are comparable with those which confronted the house four years ago when this measure was enacted.
I stress again that the one effective limitation in this act upon the powers of the minister, the time limitation, is to be eliminated 50433-121
Defence Production Act by the measure foreshadowed by this resolution. The government offers no limitation in its place.
Let me make it as clear as I can that we of Her Majesty's loyal opposition are prepared to give such powers as are required in support of the defence program, and as are proper for a parliament to confer upon a government in relation to a matter as important as defence in times like these, taking account both of the dangers in the world today and the extent to which we are better equipped today than we were when this measure was first enacted to face those dangers. We are prepared to see adequate powers provided. We do not propose to put any factious obstacle in the way of the proper carrying out of a necessary defence program.
But, sir, if hon. members will thoroughly study this act and appreciate the full scope of the powers that it confers, they will certainly see that there are powers in the act for the extension of which, under conditions now existing, there is no adequate justification given by the government. We are prepared to give adequate powers. We are not prepared to support the conferring of sweeping powers, virtually dictatorial powers upon the government. Let hon. members, if they will between the time this resolution is discussed and the time the bill will come before us, ponder well upon the true effect of the very brief bill that will be introduced, involving the re-enactment and the reconferring upon the government, without even a time limitation, of these vast powers.
The course the government ought to follow now, in my submission, Mr. Chairman, is to revise the bill they propose to introduce following this resolution, and to substitute a bill which will reconfer only those powers that are really necessary to the continuation of the defence program under existing circumstances. They should withdraw that portion of the proposed bill which would have the effect of giving unlimited extension to powers which are so broad that no case has been made for their extension in their present form. I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution seems to be a bit of a grab-bag, in that it deals with three more or less unrelated matters.
First of all, there is a change in the grading of Durum wheat and soybeans, which I understand has been recommended, and so

far as I know carries the approval of people interested in growing those crops. I think there is perhaps very little question as to that phase of the resolution and the bill which will be founded upon it. I believe however that I could speak with more intelligence in the matter after seeing the bill and its provisions.
Then, secondly, there is the provision for the addition of another commissioner to the board of grain commissioners. The parliamentary assistant has said that this new commissioner is to be for the province of Saskatchewan. I would hope that the recommendations made by various farm organizations over many years to the effect that there should be farmer representation not only on this board but on the wheat board, as well as on other boards dealing with agricultural products, might be followed in connection with this new appointment. In other words, I would hope that the appointee would be an active farmer and one who would represent the views and interests of those people who are actually growing the grain with which the board of grain commissioners deals.
I was not clear as to the meaning of what was said by the parliamentary assistant when he pointed out that the new commissioner is to be for Saskatchewan. It is not clear whether he is to deal only with grain matters in that province, and not act as a member of the whole board, or whether he is to function in some other capacity.
My understanding has been that the board of grain commissioners in the past has acted as a board, and while one commissioner might have more jurisdiction in regard to a certain area, and another greater jurisdiction in another area, in the result they acted as a group in dealing with the general questions coming before them connected with the grading of grains.
Perhaps the parliamentary assistant would tell us exactly what the composition of the board will be, and whether there will be any changes in the duties of the various commissioners as a result of the appointment of the new one.
The third matter mentioned in the resolution is the increase in salaries. This would seem to be in line with what has been going on for some time past in connection with other government boards. Last year increases were made in the salaries of the pension commissioners and legislation has been before the house recently making provision for increases in the remuneration of members of the war veterans allowance board. I would assume that this increase is in line with those others which have been made in connection with members on other government boards.

However, inasmuch as an extra member is to be appointed to the board, and presumably the duties of the other members would be reduced because of that new appointment, one wonders whether this is the appropriate time to increase their salaries. In other words, apparently they are going to be given more money to do less work.
It may be that in view of the general increases in salaries of members of government boards in recent years, these commissioners should also have increases so that their salaries would be brought into line with those of other board members.
I will reserve my position and that of this party until we see the bill and learn something more about what the changes in duties will be.

I was just going to remind the government that had they amended the act I would not be presenting my bill. This resolution precedes the presentation of a bill to amend the grain act which will amend the statutory grades of western grain and eastern grain with respect to the grade No. 3 amber Durum wheat. These amendments will have to be studied when the bill is brought down, and we shall then be able to judge whether the provisions suggested are in the best interests of the wheat producers.
The resolution suggests that there shall be established grades of soybeans as recommended by the committee on western and eastern grain standards. I have no doubt that that suggestion will be a valuable one, particularly to the areas of Canada like Ontario where soybeans are an important crop.
The Canada Grain Act has a long history. It was placed on the statute books of this country first in 1912. It was preceded by the Manitoba grain act, which was placed on

Canada Grain Act
the statute books in 1900. The Manitoba grain act was placed on the statute books of this country only after the wheat producers had fought a long and hard battle to get some regulation in the grading of wheat and other grains. It was found inadequate and finally in 1912 the Canada Grain Act was placed on the statute books. The present act was given a thorough overhaul in 1930. I suggest it is time again that major amendments were made to this act so that it can function in the interests of the producers much better than it is now doing.
A number of amendments to this act have been suggested from time to time. One of the suggestions was made to the agricultural committee last year by Mr. G. A. Mills, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool employees association. In his presentation to the committee he pointed out that local elevator agents are often required to work 16 hours a day, and some days even longer. Mr. Mills readily admitted that with the present congestion on the prairies some work days were indeed very short; but he presented what I considered to be a reasonable and fair case for an amendment to the Canada Grain Act that would give reasonable working conditions to the elevator agents. He was fair in his representation on behalf of the Saskatchewan wheat pool employees. He said that the elevator agents would not mind working extra hours in harvest time when the demand on elevator space was very great, but he asked parliament to amend the Canada Grain Act to provide reasonable working hours and a reasonable work week for elevator agents and employees. The request was fair and was something that the government should have considered.
The Canada Grain Act establishes a body of regulations; it sets out grades for the grading, storage, transportation and marketing of western grain. The act which establishes grades regulates the grain trade. It regulates the grain only from the farm to Port Arthur-Fort William, Vancouver or Churchill when the grain is going into domestic consumption. When the grain is going into the export market, the Canadian grades are continued from the local elevator point to the ultimate consuming nation. The good grading system which prairie farmers support, and which they are glad to see in operation, ends on grain that is consumed in Canada when it leaves the prairie area. Therefore, Canadians in Ontario, in Quebec, in the maritimes and in British Columbia are unable to take advantage of the excellent grade standards that are set out in the Canada Grain Act. If I were a member from a province outside the prairies, and if I were

representing an agricultural constituency, I would ask in this house that the same grade standards set out in the Canada Grain Act be continued on grain through the retail outlets in those other provinces in Canada for the benefit of the people.
I have seen some of the kinds of grain sold in Ontario that the trade have the effrontery to call feed oats or feed barley, and it is really just a conglomeration of weed seeds and screenings. It is something that I would say is scarcely fit for animal consumption, and it is no wonder that the feeder in eastern Canada believes he is really getting beaten when he buys prairie grains and gets grain of that standard. I believe that the good standards that are established for Canadian grain on the prairies should be carried right down to the feeder in Ontario, in Quebec, in the maritime provinces and in British Columbia. Why should grain that has been segregated be mixed and have placed in it weed seeds, noxious weeds of all kinds, and then finally be sold to the feeders in eastern Canada? It hurts not only the feeder who is buying the grain, but the whole grain business in Canada. The main advantage of this suggestion would be to the feeder, but it is an advantage that would carry right back to the grain producer if the grade standards that are put into effect first at the local elevator are carried right through to the feeder in this part of Canada. I hope that before this discussion ends hon. members outside the prairies will stand up in this house and ask the government to extend the provisions of this excellent act so that their farmers can receive the benefit of it.
I know that some hon. members think that the grain producers sometimes get too much from the government. We in this group do not believe that at all. If we get in some respects anything resembling justice it is because over the years now for a number of generations representatives from western Canada have battled in this house for the kind of legislation we are discussing tonight. If representatives from other parts of Canada would stand up in their places and battle on behalf of the feeders and farmers in their constituencies I suggest that they too would get some of the excellent legislation that applies now to western Canada.
The battle to obtain the Canada Grain Act was not an easy one. As a matter of fact the Canada Grain Act was placed on the statute books after the first historic siege of Ottawa by prairie farmers in 1910. History relates that about 1,000 western farmers came to Ottawa to demand a better system of grading the grain they were producing. As a result of

that delegation and the inquiry which followed, we had placed upon the statute books in 1912 the first Canada Grain Act.
I suggest to the government that unless some amendments, particularly the one I have mentioned already, are forthcoming, the day may come when the prairie producers will find that their only alternative, that the only course they can follow, will be to once again come to Ottawa in a body to place before the government their requests that justice be done.
I do not know of any group in this country outside of producers who when they produce a commodity and when they sell a commodity are forced by circumstances to do business with a certain organization or a certain corporation. Because of the need of amendments to this act prairie producers are being forced to take their grain to elevators with which they would not do business if they had a free choice. I made that statement before the agriculture committee last year when the members of the board of grain commissioners showed that they did not have a full or thorough knowledge of the act they were administering.
