subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Hon. members should realize that they can ask questions only with the permission of the hon. member who has the floor. It is of course not within the competence of the chairman to insist that an answer be given. I also must remind hon. members that the hon. member who has the floor should not be interrupted without his consent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The resolution before us asks that the chairman of the board-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: I should like the hon. member to indicate which member of the board of grain commissioners he considers to be inefficient; please name him.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
All of them. The one I am referring to at the moment is the chairman, who gets the largest salary, which salary is to be increased by this resolution from $14,000 to $15,000 a year.
There are such things, and these things have to occur, as overages in country elevators. These overages appear at the end of the year when the inventory is taken. The inventory and the records of the company show whether there is an overage or a shortage. During the last number of years overages have appeared

Canada Grain Act
quite frequently and the farmers union representing the farmers of western Canada have asked that certain steps be taken in relation to overages.
I welcomed the announcement of the parliamentary assistant that from now on overages in grain terminals will not be considered the property of Her Majesty but will be turned over to the Canadian wheat board so that the funds from the overages may be used for the advantage of agriculture from which they arose instead of going into the general revenues of the government. Last year before the agriculture committee we had asked the board of grain commissioners about these overages. I asked the chairman whether it was possible for a member of the committee to get a report of the overages in country elevators and he said yes. He said, "Just ask me and I will give you that information". I then asked him if a farmer could obtain the same information. This evidence is shown at page 222 of the report of the committee on agriculture and colonization for 1954. He said yes, the members of the committee could obtain the information and a farmer could obtain the information.
One of the main purposes of the Canada Grain Act is to see to it that there are not continuous huge overages shown by the grain trade; because if there are huge overages shown, they have been taken from somebody and they have not been paid for. There is only one place they could be taken from and that is from the producer himself. That is the main reason we now have such a thing as the Canada Grain Act, namely because farmers over the years have had taken from them excess dockage which has resulted in excess overages.
So we asked the chairman if this information could be made available and his answer was yes. He admitted that he had been administering the act for a long time and that he had dealt with hundreds upon hundreds of cases of shortages and overages by country elevators. One would have expected him to be completely conversant not only with the act but with his own practice. But the next day he rose before the committee and said, "I was wrong yesterday; I have to admit I was wrong. If somebody requests that overages be disclosed, I will not be able to divulge that information".
The hon. member for Winnipeg South asked which member I had been referring to and whether I had considered them all to be inefficient. We were still discussing the matter of overages, when Mr. Roy Milner, one of the commissioners, attempted to explain why overages exist and how they came about. Of all the statements made before that committee, his statement was the most amazing

one and as the committee went on, it was the one that was clearly shown could not be substantiated in fact. He said that one reason why overages occurred was because of what he said was the fact-and we disagreed with him-namely, that often elevator agents will strike a bargain with a producer whereby a producer allows the elevator agent to take excess dockage in return for an upgrading of the producer's grain. We said we did not think that was done.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware of the fact that the gentleman to whom he is referring has spent his whole life in the grain trade and presumably knows what he is talking about?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
That is the whole point. Here is a man who knew all about the grain trade from A to Z. He has spent years in it. I am not sure, but I believe it was with such a large company as the Alberta-Pacific Company in Alberta. It may have been some other line elevator company. He did not say that he knew of one or two cases in his vast experience. Oh no; not the gentleman that I am talking about. He said this, as reported at page 251:
In the buying of grain in country elevators dockage is an important feature. There have been a good many instances in the country elevator where a farmer is agreeable to allow some higher percentage of dockage if he can get a higher grade. You must know of cases of that kind-it is done every day.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: I have never heard of it!

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: I have been in the business all my life, Mr. Argue, and I have heard of it a thousand times-there is just a difference of opinion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Which one are you going to take?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
In this case I take my own because I think my opinion was correct, and I think I can prove it. Not only do I think that Mr. Roy Milner was completely wrong but I think that by his very suggestion he was saying that he as a member of the board of grain commissioners was not doing his part to see that the provisions of the Canada Grain Act were adequately enforced. To reinforce my point I quote section 156 of the Canada Grain Act, 1930:
156. Everyone who, either generally or in any particular transaction relating to grain, induces or attempts to induce the manager of any elevator, or any person acting on behalf of such manager, to state the incorrect weight of any grain delivered into or out of such elevator, or to claim excessive dockage from any such grain, shall be liable on summary conviction to imprisonment for not more than six months or a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars.

Because of that statement or mainly because of that statement-but whether because of that statement or for some other reason; and the minister did his part in this matter-we had called before that committee representatives of the main grain elevator companies in Canada; and the members of the C.C.F. group in the agriculture committee asked each and every one of those representatives- among whom were included representatives of the wheat pool, United Grain Growers Limited, and Mr. Cecil Lamont, president of North-West Line Elevators Association-this question: What is the attitude of your elevator company towards elevator agents taking excessive dockage in the way suggested by Mr. Milner?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: The whole thing depends on the term "excessive". What do you mean by "excessive"?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I thought my hon. friend had some knowledge of the grain business. If I haul in to the elevators a load of grain that, by gross weight, has 100 bushels in the load, but by weight there are in it 2 per cent of wild oats and 98 bushels of wheat, then the correct dockage is 2 per cent. But if somebody tries to take 5 per cent of dockage off the cash ticket when there is only 2 per cent of dockage in the load, that is excessive dockage.
I am glad to point out to the house that the representatives of each of these grain companies without exception said that their specific instructions to their elevator agents were to take the correct dockage and to give the correct weight. They said that at no time did they condone an elevator agent's taking the wrong dockage and giving the wrong weight.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Have you not heard of the swing of the beam?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: My hon. friend apparently knows something about the grain business. Now he is in with the swing of the beam. I am not referring to the swing of the beam. The swing of the beam can do things to the farmers that it should not be allowed to do. The farmer should get the correct weight and the correct dockage. The elevator companies in Canada repudiated the evidence of a commissioner of the board of grain commissioners. Yet the gentleman in question is going to get a salary increase of from $12,000 to $13,500.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: He is worth every cent of it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
He is worth every cent of it? He is the transport controller, and I could do
Canada Grain Act
all the transport controlling he has done, I am sure each day, on the telephone in a few minutes before breakfast.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: What a man.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
He is not, in fact, controlling the distribution of box cars at local elevator points. I cannot refer to that subject. Here we have a member of the board of grain commissioners who is not an acting member but merely listed on staff, and he is to be given an increase from $12,000 to $13,500. Then there is to be another person on the board of grain commissioners who comes from Saskatchewan. He is a newly appointed member. His name is Stanley Loptson, and from what I have read in the press he is a director of the United Grain Growers. I should like the parliamentary assistant to list his qualifications in detail. What are the qualifications of the new member of the board of grain commissioners? Was his appointment recommended by the three western wheat pool organizations that represent the producers in the grain business in western Canada? I ask further if his appointment was recommended by the farmers union of the three prairie provinces or, someone suggests, the federation of agriculture of which the western pools are a part.
The Canada Grain Act is important, and surely appointments to the board of grain commissioners should be made after the most thorough and complete consultation with the western farm organizations. The person appointed to the board should be a man who is qualified and not somebody who is appointed for political reasons and purposes. I am all too fearful that now as in the past these appointments are governed not by what people know but by whom they know. This is not the only board that has political appointees, good friends of the government, good friends of the Liberal party, good friends of the Minister of Agriculture-yes, good friends of the people whom he supports at various Liberal conventions that take place from time to time.
The personnel of this board is, as I have said, very important and we need the best qualified people to act as commissioners and chief commissioners. I know personally quite a number of outstanding farm leaders in western Canada who I believe would make excellent members of such a board. What I have said should not be taken to mean that I believe all the officials of the board of grain commissioners are inefficient. As a matter of fact the most efficient are paid a good deal less salary than some of the others. I might refer to Dr. J. A. Anderson, the chief chemist, whose salary is not $13,500 or $15,000 but is $8,600. There is a man who is highly

Canada Grain Act
qualified and suited to the position he occupies. There is no question in my mind at all that he was the outstanding witness from the board of grain commissioners before the committee. It did not take a salary of $15,000 a year to attract this efficient man to serve his country and the agricultural producers in the capacity of chief chemist of the board of grain commissioners.
Most of the proposals of the government as outlined in the resolution on the order paper may be acceptable but not the final proposal for a salary increase. I believe that is something that is unwarranted, unjustified and should not be granted. I believe that the government if it wished could, with the existing level of salaries, man the board of grain commissioners with competent men who have been recommended by the producers of western Canada and who would do an outstanding job in taking care of the business of the farmers in administering an act that has often been referred to as the Magna Carta of the western grain producers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am going to be quite brief in my remarks-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: The hon. member for Fort William.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise now because anyone who lives at the lakehead where we have the breadbasket of the world, about 30 elevators, knows something about the character and ability of the grain commissioners. I have often been in their office and I have brought many questions to them. Not very long ago I presented to them the case of a young man who I thought should not be dismissed, and I received courteous and efficient treatment. I pay my tribute to the board of grain commissioners in Winnipeg as men who are doing an outstanding job. I consider the hon. member who has just spoken as a personal friend, but when he dares to stand up in the house and say that the members of the board are receiving salaries that they are not earning I think he is going beyond what he should say.
The hon. member also said that there might be a trek of farmers to Ottawa unless something else happens. Anybody who listened to the debate in the house yesterday saw how far away from the mark so many of the opposition members were and listened to the Minister of Agriculture straighten them out. As long as we have the present Minister of Agriculture the farmers of western Canada are going to be well represented. I pay my tribute not only to the minister but to the efficiency, character and ability of the grain commissioners.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 am going to be quite brief in my remarks because I think we will be in a better position to consider this matter after the bill is brought down. I say that particularly in view of the fact that apparently there are going to be certain things in the bill that are not mentioned in the resolution, for instance, the question of overages. The hon. member for Fort William was very strong in his defence of the board of grain commissioners. Perhaps if the member were a grain producer he would not support them quite so strongly. I know that some members may say that the farmers are always grousing. There is one point of great interest in that regard. The farmers of western Canada have nothing but praise for the operation of the wheat board but they have nothing but criticism for the operation of the board of grain commissioners. There must be some reason for that, and if it were just a matter of their criticizing for the sake of criticizing they would also be criticizing the operation of the wheat board.
Time and again they have said that in their opinion the wheat board is a very efficient organization and they have nothing but praise for the chairman of the board. We in this group are glad that there is to be an increase in the number of assistant grain commissioners from three to four. We were glad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that recommendations had been sought from the various farm organizations because we took for granted that the government would, if at all possible, accept the recommendations of these organizations in making any appointment. But from what we hear now apparently they have decided to put a man on the board who may not meet with the approval of the majority of the farm organizations. I think it was mentioned that one farm organization has supported a certain appointment, but it would be very interesting to know which organization it is because there are many so-called farm organizations that in reality do not represent the producers at all.
Now, the interprovincial farm union has for a number of years asked that additional assistants be appointed because it was felt the board was understaffed, and that that was probably the reason they were not able to carry out their duties more efficiently

in the opinion of the union, at any rate. On many occasions they criticized the fact that they were not able to get information, and the records they repeatedly requested, as well as information regarding grading and shipments. They were critical also of the board regarding the question of overages.

I was glad to hear the parliamentary assistant say that an amendment would be introduced to provide that the proceeds from the sale of overages in the terminal elevators would be turned over to the farmers. I take it these funds will be turned over to the wheat board instead of being turned over to the general revenue fund as has been the practice in the past.
When we are on the question of overages, I may say that we are interested in the overages in the country elevators. I agree pretty well with everything the member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) said on that matter. After all, the country elevators are merely the agents of the wheat board. As agents of the wheat board, I cannot see why they should be rewarded for short-weighting the farmers, for overdocking them or for receiving an excess amount of shrinkage allowance. Unless they are doing some of those things, it is difficult to understand why these large overages exist. The proceeds from those overages certainly do not belong to the line elevator companies; they are the property of the farmer.
These line elevator companies, operating as agents of the wheat board, have no right whatever to keep the proceeds from these overages. I am hoping, therefore, that the government will go one step further. They are now providing that the proceeds from these overages in the terminal elevators shall be turned over to the farmers instead of the general revenue fund. The next step is to see that the proceeds from the sale of overages in the country elevator companies shall be turned over also to the wheat board so the farmers may benefit to the full extent from the sale of their produce.
I have sold a lot of grain in my time. I know there is absolutely no sense or reason to the type of dockage which the farmer has to put up with from time to time. Any time there is a run on the elevators, that is when a heavy volume of grain is going into the elevators, you invariably find that dockage is heavier than at other times. I might refer to my own operations on my farm by saying that we put a cleaner on our combine. We were bringing grain into the elevator that did not have any weed seeds in it at all, yet I was still getting about 2 or 3 per cent dockage. I took the cleaner off because I thought if I was going to be docked for clean grain I might as well put the weed seeds in the grain. We took the cleaner off and the dockage was still the same. In my opinion, this proves that they just had a standard minimum dockage, and it did not matter whether or not your grain was clean, you were going to be charged that dockage.
Canada Grain Act
Sometimes when the weed seeds are quite heavy the dockage will go up to 14 per cent, especially when pig weed seeds are prevalent.
I notice that the interprovincial farm unions are asking for an exhaustive investigation into the operation of the grain trade I shall read what they say:
However, we are convinced more than ever, following the questioning of the present board of grain commissioners by members of the agricultural committee of the House of Commons last year, that there is an urgent need for a complete and exhaustive inquiry into the whole question of grain grading and handling, since the question of ever-increasing grain overages by weight and grade is by no means solved, nor is the practice of allowing diversion charges settled.
It is quite a while now since we had an investigation of that kind, and I think it would do a lot to help restore confidence if such an investigation were carried out. If everything is all right the investigation will disclose that, and if there are things happening which should not be happening the investigation will show what steps can be taken to see that irregularities of that kind are not continued.
I also agree wholeheartedly with what the member for Assiniboia said about trying to carry the grades right through to the east. We had a lot of evidence in the agriculture committee two years ago that many of these eastern feeders were having to buy as No. 5 wheat what was actually only feed wheat. They brought samples of the grain to prove their point. The samples were not sealed and it might be argued that the grain had been deliberately mixed. I do not think that would be done because they would not gain anything. Any of us familiar with grain realized upon looking at these samples that these people had had to buy as No. 5 wheat what was in reality only poor feed. That is certainly not fair to the farmers of eastern Canada, and it is certainly not fair to the western farmers because the farmers in eastern Canada get the idea that the grain we are raising is of very poor quality.
These are some of the things I feel ought to be dealt with at this time. There is one other point. Many people say, if you are so dissatisfied with the way the line elevator companies are operating why do you not haul your grain to the pool elevators? If you haul your grain to the pool elevator and that elevator makes any undue profits, then the proceeds would be returned to you through the participation certificate. This would be true if the farmers were able to deliver their grain to the elevator of their choice. Unfortunately, that is not the case. Owing to the fact the elevators are plugged, and owing to the fact that cars are allocated evenly amongst

Canada Grain Act
the elevators instead of being allocated to those elevators to which the most grain is going, the farmers are not able to deliver their grain to the elevator of their choice. Now, I am trespassing on the resolution of the hon. member for Assiniboia, so I will not say more on that question. I am hoping he will be bringing that resolution before the house in the near future so we can discuss it. I shall not say any more until the bill is introduced.

speechtext: The member for Assiniboia made what I consider an excellent case, but there are a few points I should like to emphasize. During the period I was away from parliament, from 1949 to 1953, I had to earn my bread by the sweat of my brow.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: You must have gone hungry.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: I am not sorry.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: No thanks to you, if he did.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
In 1950, we were confronted with an unusually early frost, and excessive moisture created a condition that was unknown in our area. With a group of farmers I went to see the experts of the grain commission. We received some excellent advice from them. They told us we had better get this grain out of our granaries and away to the driers before spring or in all probability it would go out of condition. We were grateful for their advice. They saved the farmers in the area a good deal of money.
We asked them why they were not giving all the farmers the information that they had given to us. They said, you see the work that is piled up ahead of us and we are not responsible for publicity. It is our job to do the testing. We have the information, but you have to go to the other office to look into the publicity angle. Our next appointment, therefore, was with Allan McLean, one of the assistant commissioners. Mr. McLean was not ready to see us for some time, but when he did see us he was well briefed from Winnipeg, I presume from Dr. Anderson. He had all the answers we wanted and promised that the board would get the information out to the farmers in the area concerning the necessity of getting this grain off the farms and to the driers before spring.
One of the farmers in the group had known Mr. McLean for many years, and he was not surprised that a commercial traveller for a grocery firm really would not know any more about the problem than Mr. McLean did. Some time later all the commissioners were in Saskatoon at the annual meeting of the farmers union. The question of overages came up at the convention and the farmers, rightly or wrongly, felt that they had been

taking a fleecing through the years and that the board of grain commissioners should give them greater protection. I do not want to get in wrong with my neighbour, the hon. member for Winnipeg South who sits beside me, and who is making a better defence for the grain trade tonight than the government members are making. But, rightly or wrongly, the farmers on the prairies who have been selling grain for 50 years are convinced that they have not got a square deal.
Mr. McKenzie, chairman, made it quite clear that they were policemen who were not afraid of the consequences, that they really were tough. And I was interested to find out just how tough they were. I ventured to ask the question: "Have you taken legal action against any of the offenders?" "Why, certainly we have." "How many, in the last five years?" "Well, I have not that information here, but I will get it for you." "Well, you will likely remember one case. Can you not think of one case?" And then Mr. McKenzie said, "Well, we do not consider it wise to disclose the dealings with individual grain companies. We deal with all the companies, and it is not good public relations to make public the problems we have."
I think the farmers are justified in sharing the dissatisfaction expressed so well by the hon. member for Assiniboia, when he says that the board of grain commissioners are not coming clean with the farmers, and telling them how much the companies have been taking by way of overages throughout the years, and what is being done to protect the farmers.
Personally, we sell all our grain through the pool. While we would like to have an exact accounting of the grain we deliver, we know that if the pool does have overages, eventually all the pool members will get the benefit therefrom. But those who have the misfortune to have to sell their grain to nonpool companies do not get the benefits the pool members get from overages.
We have a responsibility to see that more complete information is supplied to farm organizations and individual farmers regarding the number of bushels of No. 3 that the Searle elevator company for example buys in a year, and the number of bushels of No. 3 it sells in that time.
I know that the pool organization tries to have its agents buy grain on a fair basis. They do not want to take advantage of any of their customers. However, sometimes agents have overages, while at other times they are short. But as I said before, the pool organization does pass on to the members any benefits that might accrue.
Another point made by the hon. member for Assiniboia which, in my opinion, should be

emphasized is that the farmers in western Canada at the moment are facing the greatest crisis since the thirties. Yet this government comes along and asks that the chief commissioner's salary be increased from $14,000 to $15,000, and that the salaries of the other commissioners be increased from $12,000 to $13,500.
Just this week we were told by the government that $840 per year for a single veteran or $1,440 for a married veteran was a very generous settlement by the people of Canada to a veteran of world war I. How can we tell the veterans of world war I, who are farmers, that $840 a year is ample for them, but that the chairman of the board of grain commissioners cannot get along on $14,000 a year, and that his salary has to be increased to $15,000; or that the others, who are getting $1,000 per month, are really up against it, and that they have to have another $1,500 a year to supplement their incomes?
I submit that if this government did not have its overwhelming majority, and if it did not disregard completely public opinion in all parts of Canada, it would not dare come before parliament at this time asking for increases of these proportions.
Then, there is one further point which thus far in the debate has not been mentioned. Farmers resent very much the fact that boards in general, and this board in particular, is nothing less than an organization of favoured political servants of the government. In the Leader-Post for Friday, February 25, there is a picture on the front page bearing the caption "Stanley Loptson Goes to the Grain Board". It says:
Stanley Loptson, 42, of Bredenbury, only son of Asmundur Loptson, Liberal member for Saltcoats in the Saskatchewan legislature has been appointed a member of the board of grain commissioners.
And for the benefit of those who are not familiar with the name Loptson, I might explain that Mr. Asmundur Loptson succeeded the hon. member for Rosthern as leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan when that hon. member came to Ottawa some time ago, and fulfilled that role very well until the convention was held last year. And this is Stanley, the only son. I know nothing about him, but I think it is scandalous that the son of the Liberal leader should take on a job paying $13,500, when he has no qualifications for that job.
The hon. member for Assiniboia referred to Dr. Anderson, a very distinguished gentleman who enjoys the confidence of grain producers and of scientists all across Canada. How can Dr. Anderson respect his boss, who knows nothing about the problems the commissioners 50433-1224
Canada Grain Act
should be facing, a boss who walks in on top of the others, at a salary of $13,500?
I have before me the Public Accounts giving the names of those employed in the grain act administration who are receiving more than $5,000 a year, but I do not read the names of any of the very capable men who gave us the information we wanted when we were confronted with a problem in 1950. None of those boys got up to $5,000.
How can we expect the fullest co-operation from those very able men who have spent 25 years of their lives in the government service, who never get as much as $5,000, and who have to take their orders from the son of the ex-Liberal leader who comes in, on the first day, at a salary of $13,500?
This is not good enough in a democracy in this year 1955-when we cannot do anything better than $840 for a single veteran who gave of his best between 1914 and 1918, or $1,440 for a married veteran.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Who recommended it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Somebody asks a good question: Who recommended it? The question has been asked about Mr. McKenzie, and I must share the views of the hon. member for Assiniboia rather than those of the hon. member for Winnipeg South. No doubt Mr. McKenzie is a very genial friend; but I saw him in action at the farmers union convention, and had to form my own opinion upon his performance before a thousand farmers in Saskatchewan. I have to take the opinion of the hon. member for Assiniboia rather than that of the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
But I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg South would not have any quarrel with me when I refer to the case of Allan McLean. He does not know Allan McLean, I should imagine; but Allan McLean was the Liberal candidate who ran against the hon. member for Yorkton in 1940. For some reason or another the farmers up in that area decided they would rather have Mr. Castle-den work for them in Ottawa than Mr. McLean.
As I said before, Mr. McLean was a commercial traveller for a grocery house, and a very genial person indeed. He was a good grocery salesman and made a lot of friends throughout the years. Later he became national organizer for the Liberal party. I do not know how good a job he did in that respect; but after he had worked at it for some time he returned to Saskatchewan, just before the 1949 election. Apparently he started on pay on March 14, 1949. Saskatchewan was a part of the dominion where the Liberals were in pretty bad shape. Unless something could be done very soon the future of the

Canada Grain Act
Minister of Agriculture was not too bright. But I resent very much the using of public funds to send the national organizer of the Liberal party into Saskatchewan under the cloak of an assistant commissioner to the grain commissioners. He started rolling as soon as he got out there. Mr. Percy Wright had a sessional paper produced in 1951 to find out just where Mr. McLean was rolling in that period prior to the election. He did not lose very much time. He of course got into Melville, then he got into Yorkton, into Melfort, into Humboldt and into Moose Jaw. He got into Swift Current and into Shaun-avon. He really got around at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. When it was all over the hon. member for Yorkton was left at home, and I was left at home. The hon. member for The Battlefords was left at home, and the hon. members for Moose Mountain, Humboldt and Swift Current were left at home. We all took our medicine. We are all going to live longer as a result of our holiday on the farm, but I think the Canadian people should know that the government of Canada takes responsibility for putting the national organizer of the Liberal party on salary in Saskatchewan. He is still there and a very generous allowance has been made for his travelling expenses.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce should recommend to the minister that, after giving an explanation as to the need for the first change suggested in this particular resolution, he make sure that he does not continue any longer a policy that has made the Minister of Agriculture so famous in Canadian politics, namely putting his organizers into positions of this sort at public expense. The western people want no more of it, and we cannot afford at this time to ask the Canadian people to increase the salaries of those Liberal organizers.

speechtext:
I would be remiss in my duty, Mr. Chairman, if I did not rise in my place and oppose this resolution and fight all the way through the bill which is to follow.
The resolution suggests that a bill is to be introduced to make three amendments to the Canada Grain Act. The first thing is that they are going to amend the statutory grades of western grain and eastern grain with respect to the grade No. 3 amber Durum wheat and all grades of soybeans as recommended by the committee on western and eastern grain standards. That is a good move. It is a thing that should be done, and I shall watch very carefully to see what the people who have bought No. 3 Durum wheat are going to do with the supplies that they have

on hand. They should be watched very carefully with respect to what they do with this No. 3 amber Durum wheat when it is made available.
Then the act is to be amended to provide for the appointment of four in lieu of three assistant grain commissioners. Well, I can only say that, after what we have heard this evening, the opinion of western farmers would be that they should be careful with respect to the kind of men they appoint to that job. If they are not to be any better than they have been in the past we will oppose it very strenuously.
The third amendment is to increase the annual salaries of the chief and the other two commissioners from $14,000 and $12,000 to $15,000 and $13,500, respectively. The board of grain commissioners is a very important one today. Very few people, except those who have been brought up in the west and understand farm operations and the growing of grain and the millions of people in those western provinces whose very livelihood depends on the grade of grain that they get, the prices they get for it and the way the grain is handled, realize how vital this is to the people of that part of the country. If hon. members had lived there for 50 years, as I have, and had watched that country grow and had seen those people carry on a battle against the private grain trade, against the private elevator companies, against the Winnipeg grain exchange which took their grain, they would understand the position. When the farmer hauled his grain in he had very little to say about the grade. He had to take whatever was offered to him. He had no resources. He was in debt and needed the money, and he sold his grain. Through years of fighting, years of struggle, he got the wheat board established and the Canada Grain Act enacted. The Canada Grain Act protected his interests. It was supposed to ensure to him the proper grades of wheat that he produced. He is sometimes still in doubt as to the actual grades, but a tremendous improvement has taken place.
When the grain was bought he had no means of telling exactly the weight of the grain that came in. As a result of his fight over the years he established the co-operative wheat pool which handled his own grain, and the profits that were made out of the handling of his grain were then returned to him in a proper co-operative manner, because the profits out of the co-operative were returned to the producer in a proper form. The Canadian wheat board returned to him the price of his grain less the cost of handling. The act is a policeman over the operations

of the grain trade in western Canada consisting of a large number of private grain companies and wheat pools that have their terminal elevators, storage facilities, grading facilities and all the rest of it. This board has carried on that work. It is a tremendous job. In some years it is quite complicated.
It is also important to see that the farmer's interest is properly carried out, properly maintained and looked after when his grain is sold and when it is mixed. There are mixing possibilities in the grain trade which the farmer discovered after he went into the business himself. One of the duties of the board of grain commissioners is to see that the mixing, the overages, the handling, the protein content and all the rest of it are properly policed.
A report has been given this evening on the qualifications of the board of grain commissioners and their appointment. It is little wonder that representatives from the west are opposed to this resolution. There is only one thing they can do. It is very difficult to see how the western grain grower can have confidence in this board in the light of the things that have been recorded this evening and the facts with regard to the appointments. I should like to read into the record a part of the report of the board of grain commissioners of last year to show some of the difficulties:
In accordance with sections 139 and 140 of the Canada Grain Act, 28 terminals and 21 eastern elevators were weighed over during the 1952-53 crop year. Due to large stocks in store, the board deferred weighovers at 18 terminals and 5 eastern elevators under authority of section 141 of the Canada Grain Act, and weighovers of 2 elevators at the Pacific coast which came due shortly after a labour strike were deferred beyond the 22 month period by the transport controller by authority granted him under the Emergency Powers Act.
Since then we have not had a report on the rest of it, and the people are just wondering what the situation is. If the overweighs are not properly recorded, if full and complete reports are not tabled sufficiently early so that the farmers have a record of exactly what has happened to their grain, they can be filled only with suspicion as to what has happened.
To show the extent of the suspicion which exists I would refer hon. members to a submission made by the Interprovincial Farm Union Council when they appeared last year before the agriculture committee. They said:
As on former occasions, we once again register strong protest against the continued late tabling of the annual report of the board of grain commissioners. The crop year closes on July 31. Even allowing as much time as three months to complete their final returns and receive grain company reports, surely it should be possible to have the report ready by December 1 or December 15 at
Canada Grain Act
the latest. There seems no good and sufficient reason why it could not, and should not, be tabled in the House of Commons as soon as the session re-convenes in January.
Then they indicate that they would like to have the opportunity of presenting their brief to the agriculture committee after having had an opportunity of looking at the annual report of the board of grain commissioners That report is late again this year. They continue:
We strongly urge that the aforementioned and all other points and factors having direct or indirect bearing on the question of grain handling as it affects both the producer and consumer be referred by the government to the agricultural committee of the House of Commons for further study. We were interested and pleased to note that this committee, in their concluding report to parliament during the last session, recommended a further study of the operations of the Canada Grain Act. We trust that, in adopting the report, the house recognized parliament's continued responsibility. May we officially request that before making such a review advance notice be given in ample time for the farm unions to make their representation to this important committee on a subject of such vital importance to agriculture.
That is the way they feel about grain handling and grading.
We feel the information brought out at the agricultural committee of the House of Commons last year is, in itself, sufficient justification for a full-fledged inquiry by an independent commission (on which the producers would be adequately represented) into grain grading, weighing, mixing, handling and storing-from the time delivery is made to the country elevators by farmers right through to sale to the ultimate consumers.
As I have said, this is too important a board, a board which is too vitally concerned with this important matter, not to have represented on it the grain growers of the west. There are representatives of the line companies and the elevator companies, but the pool organizations have suffered in the handling of grain and the quantities they have been allowed to handle. There is too much of this political type of appointment going on. Apparently it has already been settled as to who will take the place of Mr. Vallance, who is retiring from the board.
When amendments to the Canada Grain Act are being considered I would urge strongly that this type of appointment be stopped; that people who have been strongly recommended by the large farm organizations in the west should be placed on this board in sufficient number in order to do a job and do it right; that a complete report should be tabled every year and on time, and that a full opportunity be given representatives of these organizations to go back and give their reports to the farm organizations as representing the farmers.
Needed amendments would give representation to the pool organizations which handle

Canada Grain Act
as much as 50 per cent of the grain in our province but which at present have no representation on the board. They should be represented rather than the elevator companies.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I consider it a great honour to have the privilege of speaking on this measure this evening. I want to say quite frankly that I played no part in giving ideas to this or former governments in connection with the Canada Grain Act, which is under discussion tonight. I take it that the Canada Grain Act is the result of representations made by farm organizations and farm members who put their ideas before the house as to the kind of act we should have in relation to the marketing of our grain so it would work to the best benefit of the producer and consumer alike.
Over the years no particular political party or group can take credit for the present grain act. While this is a good act I believe it can be improved. What I want to say right now is that we who speak for western agriculture are going to insist that it operate in the interests of those for whom it was set up, namely, the agricultural people of this country.
The fact remains that the government is introducing this evening a measure which contains several ideas. First, the resolution makes reference to No. 3 amber Durum wheat and all grades of soybeans and it is recommended that the grading of these be changed as recommended by the committee on western and eastern grain standards. Further on it provides for the addition of another assistant grain commissioner, there being three under the present act. It then goes on to state that it is proposed to increase the salary of the chief commissioner from $14,000 to $15,000, and the salaries of the other two commissioners from $12,000 to $13,500.
My experience in the grain business goes back to early childhood. My first recollection is when I was hardly big enough to be lifted onto a high grain wagon to drive four horses with grain to the elevator. I can remember delivering grain in the twenties and even before that. I remember my father would come out from the elevator shaking his head and wondering why he got the grade he did. As
[Mr. Castleden.l
hon. members in this group have stated already, oftentimes a farmer because of certain conditions would receive overdockage or rather heavy dockage in respect to his grain. There does not seem to be much reason for that.
I remember an incident some years ago when a neighbour of mine took the trouble to take a sample of the wheat which he shipped that year and put it in a sealer which was put away on a shelf. He received No. 1 grade for that wheat during the crop season. Then in two years, as you recall-in 1951, I think it was-we had a very wet fall. Of course in our area in the province of Saskatchewan the wheat was in nearly all cases being graded No. 3 tough. We realized that in many parts of our district the wheat should have been graded straight grading and should have been graded closer to No. 1 but certainly not No. 3. Just out of curiosity they shipped a sample of this wheat which had previously graded No. 1 dry, down to Winnipeg for grading and it came back graded No. 3 tough, the same as all the wheat which was being shipped out of our area at that time.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know the reason for that situation but the western farmers are extremely suspicious, even yet, as to the fairness of the marketing of our wheat under certain conditions. I want to say this. We are quite happy in having some sort of grain act by which we can receive at least some semblance of justice. The fight has been a long one. As I indicated formerly, members representing farm areas have come to this house and put proposals before the governments in order to get an act which would give us some conformity in the marketing and grading of our western wheat. We now find that this government has not seen fit to listen to the western organizations representing farmers with a view to setting up a board of grain commissioners who are, in their opinion, familiar with the responsibility of administering the act so that justice may be done.
I am much disturbed about the new appointment being made under this resolution or the one that is proposed to be made. Just the other day on the orders of the day I asked a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. My question was with respect to the appointment to the board of grain commissioners of a new assistant commissioner. I asked what farm organizations, if any, had made a request for the appointment of Mr. Stanley Loptson. The information I received from the Minister of Trade and Commerce was that one farm organization had recommended his appointment.

I would say this, Mr. Chairman. When an important appointment such as this one is being made, the representatives of the farm organizations of western Canada should be taken into the confidence of the government and should have the opportunity to make a recommendation which would be of their choice so that we would have a commission which would be satisfactory to the farming population.
In leading off in this debate the hon. member for Assiniboia indicated that in his opinion, as a result of his experience on the parliamentary committee on agriculture, the commissioners were not capable of carrying out their duties under this act. So I join him and others who have taken the attitude that something should be done so as not to make of the board just purely a political asylum either for worn-out politicians or political friends of the Minister of Agriculture but that it should be a board representing the choice of western agriculture. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, it should be a board composed of men who have the necessary capabilities and experience and who know something about the grading and marketing of wheat. Otherwise the whole thing is going to be a farce.
I plead with the parliamentary assistant that he go to his minister and perhaps reject for the time being a further appointment. As far as I am concerned, I do not think we need an extra assistant commissioner. If we are going to do anything, we certainly should insist that those who are appointed know their job. I agree with the hon. member for Mackenzie when he asks how this government can justify making another appointment to the board and increasing the present salaries of these commissioners. The commissioner today is receiving $14,000, which is a handsome income. Each of the assistant commissioners is receiving $12,000. The proposal is to increase the salary of the chief commissioner to $15,000 and that of the assistant commissioners to $13,500.

AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Surely every member of this house must fail to see any justification for supporting this measure when-again as was stated by the hon. member for Mackenzie-just the other day, with regard to veterans of the first world war, this house could not see fit to give adequate allowances to them but felt that $840 was sufficient for a single veteran and $1,440 for a married couple.
There is something wrong with the mentality of the government when they try to foist upon the members of the House of Commons such a proposal as is indicated in
Canada Grain Act
this bill. I hope that the things that have been said by the members of this group, and those other members who have seen fit to speak on this matter to indicate that we are definitely not satisfied with this proposal, will have some effect. I think it is significant that not one single member of the government so far has risen and tried to justify the proposals contained in this resolution. I think that fact signifies that they cannot justify what they are trying to foist upon us this evening. It is my hope the whole matter will be the subject of reconsideration.
I am not so greatly concerned about the first part of the proposal to the effect that some changes shall be made in the grading of No. 3 amber Durum wheat or in respect of grades of soybeans. Maybe those changes are necessary. However, I would say this. If we want to keep faith with the producers of western Canada, surely we must at least give them some say as to who is appointed to these boards and must take some responsibility for the qualifications of these people who are appointed to the board. If that is not done, I think the farmers in western Canada may well be up in arms. They would not be exceeding their rights if they were to come down here with a delegation to meet with officials of the government, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and others, in order to try to get some justice in relation to this matter.
In closing, may I say that, after what has been said, I hope the government will seriously consider taking out of this resolution the later recommendations, namely as to the increase in salary to the present chief commissioner and the assistant commissioners and also that they will perhaps dispense with the appointment of Mr. Loptson who is already there on appointment. I think that surely such a board as this one should be outside the realm of politics. As I indicated before, I do not think it should be a political fraternity of worn-out politicians or political heelers but rather that there should be only one criterion for appointment to this board, namely the qualifications of the men who get these positions. I also want to say that we have working with the grain commissioners and under their direction a chemist-Dr. Anderson-and others who are not nearly so well paid as are the commissioners themselves. As the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out, until the commissioner and the assistant commissioners get down to business and learn what this business is all about and are able to operate the act so that it will be in conformity with their business, I would say there is no justification for bringing this measure before the house.

Canada Grain Act

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all of us in this group were extremely happy when we learned not so long ago that the resolution dealing with amendments to the wheat board act was going to be presented to the house. Certainly we were looking forward to a few radical changes and amendments that were going to mean something. We based that hope on the recommendations that were made in the committee last year by members of the committee from western Canada together with the recommendations made by the farm organizations that presented briefs to the committee. These recommendations led us to believe that something that would be of benefit to the farmers of western Canada would be incorporated in the resolution that is before us this evening. When we saw the resolution we were greatly disappointed. We had hoped, as has been said this evening, that there would be something in it about the allocation of box cars. We thought there would be something in it to deal with shortages and overages. We thought that it might involve a complete overhaul of the Canada Grain Act.
As I say, we were sadly disappointed and the farmers of western Canada were disappointed. I have had many letters from farm organizations and individual farmers in my constituency asking me if I could give them some clue as to what might be contained in the resolution that was going to be presented to the house. In their opinion the personnel of the board of grain commissioners are no longer carrying out the job that it was originally intended should be done. They feel that the board is no longer looking after the interests of the farmers of western Canada. They feel that it is quite evident from what has been going on in the last few years that the board, instead of having the interests of the farmers at heart, is primarily concerned with the interests of the line elevator companies. Certainly the evidence produced last year at the committee hearings would seem to justify that belief.
The farmers have lost confidence in the board of grain commissioners. It was obvious to all members of the committee last year that they are unable to cope in an efficient manner with the duties that they are supposed to perform. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants was one of the members of that committee. In great haste he tried to come to the rescue of the board of grain commissioners this evening and to defend the evidence they gave before the committee last year. He tried to condone the fact that they did not know what the board was printing by way of publications. He tried to make a case for the board and condone their actions with

respect to the up-grading of grain by taking excessive dockage. He tried to show that the manner in which they were carrying out the inspection of grain elevators in western Canada was quite in order in spite of the fact that Mr. Mackenzie told us that one man could only service from 500 to 600 elevators in a season. In western Canada we have over 5,400 elevator houses that need annual inspection.
One thing I thought was rather shameful was that when we tried to get some statement from the personnel of the board at the committee hearings with respect to overages in country elevators we were told that it was not in the interests of anybody to be told anything about them. They said it would not be fair to give information that a particular elevator company was taking excessive overages because it would place that elevator company in a non-competitive position with respect to the elevator nearest to it. In other words, they were not prepared to tell the farmers in one town that a certain elevator company was gypping them and stealing from them. They said it would not be fair to do so because it would place that elevator in a non-competitive position with the elevator adjacent to it. That is the kind of thing that the hon. member for Colchester-Hants, who had so much to say this evening, is trying to condone.
In spite of the fact that these men showed such incompetence, the government now has the audacity to recommend that their salaries be increased to $15,000 for the chief commissioner and $13,500 for the other commissioners. I do not think that an increase in salary will mean that any greater efficiency will be shown by the board of grain commissioners. If that were the case then possibly there would be some justification for increasing salaries. We suggest that the first thing that should be done is a complete overhaul of the Canada Grain Act. We also suggest that the next thing that should be done is to put the present grain commissioners out on pasture. It will be time then to talk about increases in salaries.
I hope when we hear more of the details concerning this legislation we will have the assurance of the minister that that part of it relating to amber Durum wheat will not mean another handout to somebody other than the producers. I am somewhat suspicious about that part of the resolution, and certainly my suspicions are well founded after the experience that all of us had in the committee last year. That suspicion has certainly been justified in the last week with the appointment of the new grain commissioner.
I am afraid that somewhere along the line'

somebody is going to benefit by placing that Durum wheat in a lower category for one reason or another because there is a great differential in price between No. 2 and a lower grade. I hope the minister will be able to assure us that is not going to happen.
I should like to say a few words about the new appointment to the board of grain commissioners. As one who has been a farmer all my life and who believes in orderly marketing, I suppose I must accept my share of responsibility along with all other farmers for having supported the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners. We believe that they are necessary organizations. These boards are only the children of the farm organizations of western Canada. I am prepared to accept my fair share of responsibility. But when I think about these men whom we have placed in positions of responsibility to do for us what should be done, appointing a man like Stanley Loptson, I hang my head in shame. This appointment was ill-conceived, ill-advised and unwarranted.
Those of us who have anything to do with grain production and are interested in the whole grain picture know that there is a big job to be done by the board of grain commissioners. We know that the present board is incapable of doing that job. I am sure that the present commissioners who looked to the minister for some help were very disappointed and frustrated when they found they were having foisted on them a man who would be of absolutely no help in carrying out what must be an arduous job for these older members of the board.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make this one observation. The recent appointment of Stanley Loptson to the board of grain commissioners proves to me conclusively that the Liberal party has learned nothing. I shall prophesy that if they continue to make these political appointments, whereby Liberal organizers roam the prairies at the taxpayers' expense, the Liberal party is doomed to extinction in western Canada.

speechtext:
Like the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, Mr. Chairman, I was pleased to note in the speech from the throne mention of the fact that the Canada Grain Act was to be amended. I supposed it was to be amended to meet the requests of the farm organizations which had asked for a complete overhaul of the Canada Grain Act. I supposed it was to be amended to meet the requests of farmers as shown by the resolution of the hon. member for Assiniboia to allow for a system of box car allocation. My disappointment was great when I noticed that rather than following these principles which
Canada Grain Act
would have met with general agreement amongst western farmers the resolution was one to increase the salaries of the commissioners and assistant commissioners of the board of grain commissioners.
A few years ago the government might have been able to make a sound argument for increasing the numbers and salaries of the board of grain commissioners. At that time farm conditions were congested and no doubt many problems would arise. However, following the assurance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that we are going to be rid of all our grain from the farms by the time this crop year is out, what is the necessity for increasing the numbers and salaries of the board of grain commissioners? The move is untimely, too, when the farmers in western Canada have just harvested the smallest crop in ten years. I feel I would be right in assuming that in most departments of government they follow the principle of promoting officials according to their ability. The junior man who has the qualifications automatically steps up as a vacancy presents itself. I believe that is a generally understood principle in most forms of business.
I wonder why it was not followed in this instance? I notice that the three assistant commissioners were completely by-passed in appointing a commissioner. I can only see one answer. It must be that the assistant commissioners were so incompetent they could not fill this position to which is attached a salary of $14,000 a year. It could be, too, that under certain circumstances this desirable principle of promotion according to ability must be disregarded for principles that are more politically expedient.
I have some evidence that would point out that perhaps the former is closer to the truth. Two years ago a complaint was made at a marketing point in my constituency that a certain elevator company was making a deduction of a half cent per bushel to be paid to a farmer who was loading grain for that company in a detached annex. There is a distinct prohibition against that in the Canada, Grain Act. I assumed that this police force, the board of grain commissioners, would be in there like an eager bird-dog investigating the situation. Finally, however, after repeated complaints from the farmers in that area, the situation was investigated. I should like to read from the report. This investigator came in from Alberta. He must have been a Fearless Fosdick or an invisible Scarlet O'Neil, because he said:
I did not contact any elevator men that day but 1 did hear all of them tell farmers who were calling that they would be able to take in grain the next morning and the earlier they got there the better.

Canada Grain Act
Here you have a man driving up with an Alberta licence on his car, not disguised, but acting as the highly paid official that he was. He did not contact any of the elevator men. He must have been standing in the driveway hidden behind a scale to hear them tell the farmers they would be able to take in grain the next day. He made a very thorough investigation of the situation.
There was another complaint, too, relating to deliveries of grain after hours. After this thorough investigation by this invisible Scarlet O'Neil from Alberta, he said:
I could not find any place where there was any discrimination. It is my personal opinion that there is nothing in this situation that a short crop or a lot of box cars would not remedy.
Then he goes on:
In view of the above circumstances, I would recommend that the file be closed.
I did not think the file should be closed, so I brought the matter before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. When I did Mr. Vallance said:
Mr. Johnson, I knew that file you were referring to as soon as you started. MacKinnon was sent into Tramping Lake. Have you got a complaint in front of you? We have none of those files with us, but I well remember this case at Tramping Lake because of the overcharge item.
Evidently the commissioners, the higher paid ones in the echelon, were familiar with the situation but deemed it undesirable, in view of the company that was involved, to make any prosecution. Mr. Milner, the other
member of the grain commission, later on said:
Could you give us that affidavit and the information? If you will do that, I will see to it that there is a prosecution launched.
Here we have one of these high paid commissioners, to whom the hon. member for Winnipeg South referred, stating that he knew all about the complaint as soon as the overcharge was mentioned, and you have the other commissioner, knowing nothing about it, but saying, You just give us the facts and we will go in there with a big wide broom and clean that mess up.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that is a good place to pause for a moment. Having pointed out that the government could not very well appoint this particular assistant commissioner to this higher paid job because of his inefficiency, I would call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

My dear Premier:
In my letter to you of January 14th, I said that I would be writing again after my return from London with a view to working out arrangements for a federal-provincial fiscal conference later this year.
Following further consideration of the matter with my colleagues, I am writing now to you to propose that we hold a preliminary
